name: Ngoreme

Amsterdam/Philadelphia: John Benjamins. doi:10.1075/cilt.338.12aun. Read in the open-access HELDA author final-draft reprint (hdl:10138/308788), 28 pp.
catalog_locator: Sec. 9 'Ngoreme', opening paragraph and infinitive rules (published p. 210; HELDA draft pp. 19-21); sec. 5 'Tone' (draft pp. 7-8); sec. 10 'Conclusion' (draft p. 23).
catalog_quote: In Ngoreme, contrastive lexical tone on both verbs and nouns is lost, and there is only one melodic tone pattern, which assigns H to the first syllable of the verb stem. However, the Ngoreme system is not that of regular stress either. In inflected verbs, there is a H tone either on the TAM markers or on the first syllable of the stem, i.e. one syllable with the highest prominence is required for each word, but the place of this prominence is morphologically determined. On the other hand, in infinitive verbs as well as in nouns, the location of the highest prominence is determined by the syllable structure. ... If the first syllable of the stem, as in (73), or the second syllable of the stem, as in (74), is heavy, the H tone is realized on the heavy syllable. ... In case both the first and the second syllables are heavy, it is the second syllable that has the H tone, as in (75). When there are no heavy syllables in the verb stem the final syllable has the H tone (76). ... In the Ngoreme variety presented here, tones are always determined either morphologically or on the syllable structure. Moreover, on the word level, Ngoreme requires at least one syllable with the highest prominence. On the other hand, the Ngoreme system is not clearly a stress system since the culminativity principle is not always satisfied as the H tones can be realized on more than one adjacent syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ngoreme (in the variety described) has no contrastive tone; each word carries one obligatory H-toned (most prominent) syllable whose position is predictable. In nouns and infinitives it is weight-driven: H goes on a heavy (long-vowel, incl. conditioned length) stem syllable -- the second if both first and second are heavy; with no heavy syllable, trisyllabic stems take stem-final H (optionally spreading to the penult or whole stem), bisyllabic and C-initial quadrisyllabic stems take stem-initial H, monosyllabic stems H. In inflected verbs the H is placed morphologically (on the TAM prefix or stem-initial syllable). Aunio explicitly says this is 'not that of regular stress' / 'not clearly a stress system' because H can sit on more than one adjacent syllable (culminativity not always met), while obligatoriness is met.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; H may spread to adjacent syllables (e.g. rising tone on heavy first syllable extended to the final in bisyllabic stems, ex. 89; free-variation spread to penult/whole stem in light trisyllabic stems).
new_statements.exceptions: Intra-Ngoreme variation: 'in the speech of some speakers, there appear to be three contrastive lexical tone patterns for bisyllabic noun stems' (sec. 9; also Aunio et al. 2019: 'some speakers have three contrastive tonal patterns'); vowel-initial quadrisyllabic stems with -ɛɛɾ/-ɛɛr take penult H (exx. 84-85); vowel-initial stems never carry H on the prefix-shared initial syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level prominence ('on the word level, Ngoreme requires at least one syllable with the highest prominence'); data are infinitives and nouns in citation/phrase-medial form (Aunio et al. 2019 note tones given are phrase-medial; utterance-final H is allowed in Ngoreme). Author frames the system as predictable H tone (privative H/zero, syllable TBU) with stress-like obligatoriness, rejecting 'pitch accent' as a type.
new_statements.identity_note: Aunio 2017 describes 'the Ngoreme variety presented here' (SIL Musoma fieldwork data, no dialect named) in which all tones are conditioned; she and Aunio et al. 2019 both note that some Ngoreme speakers retain up to three contrastive lexical tone patterns on noun stems, so the weight-determined, non-contrastive system is not uniform across the community. Laine 2023 mentions Mwibara and Rogoro dialects of Ngoreme (lexical differences only). Language identity is ngur1263 / ISO ngq throughout (Laine et al. 2025 give the glottocode explicitly).

sources.note: Sec. 2.3 'Tone and syllable structure': 'In Ngoreme and Zanaki, the lexical tones are much less stable and many speakers have shifted to penultimate stress (Zanaki) or weight-determined tone placement (Ngoreme).. In Ngoreme, some speakers have three contrastive tonal patterns'; H attracted to heavy syllables in Ngoreme infinitives (exx. 16-20, citing Aunio 2017); Ngoreme has one melodic tone (stem-initial H) and TAM-prefix H forms, no toneless verb forms; utterance-final H allowed.
